clinicalPearls: A rare normolipaemic non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis characterised by hundreds of red-brown to yellow papules and nodules with a striking predilection for flexural and intertriginous skin.
Lesions cluster symmetrically in the axillae, groin, antecubital and popliteal fossae and periorbital region, and mucous membrane involvement of the upper aerodigestive tract may occur.
Mucosal disease of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx and trachea can cause hoarseness, dysphagia or airway obstruction and is an important cause of morbidity.
Up to a third to a half of patients develop transient central diabetes insipidus from infiltration of the hypothalamic-pituitary region, which is usually mild and may remit.
Serum lipids are characteristically normal, distinguishing it from the hyperlipidaemic xanthomas it can mimic clinically.
It affects predominantly young adult males and typically follows a persistent, progressive course rather than the spontaneous involution seen in juvenile xanthogranuloma.
Histology shows a mixed infiltrate of foamy histiocytes, scattered Touton giant cells and inflammatory cells; cells are CD68 positive and CD1a negative.
An association with monoclonal gammopathy and other paraproteinaemias is reported, warranting haematological screening.
reference.pathophysiology: Xanthoma disseminatum is a proliferative disorder of macrophage-derived histiocytes belonging to the non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. Lesional histiocytes accumulate lipid to form foam cells and Touton giant cells despite normal circulating lipids, indicating that lipid uptake and storage occur locally within a reactive histiocytic infiltrate rather than as a consequence of dyslipidaemia. The cells express macrophage markers such as CD68 and factor XIIIa but not the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and langerin. The disorder is generally regarded as a reactive rather than clearly neoplastic process, although its persistence, mucosal and pituitary infiltration, and reported associations with monoclonal gammopathy suggest a dysregulated histiocytic response. Infiltration of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis interrupts vasopressin delivery to produce central diabetes insipidus, while mucosal deposits in the airway account for the potential for obstructive complications.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin)
Fasting serum lipid profile to confirm normolipaemia
Early-morning paired serum and urine osmolality and water-deprivation testing if diabetes insipidus suspected
MRI of the hypothalamic-pituitary region when endocrine features are present
Laryngoscopy or airway endoscopy if hoarseness, dysphagia or stridor
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect monoclonal gammopathy
redFlags: Hoarseness, dysphagia or stridor indicating laryngeal or tracheal mucosal involvement and potential airway compromise
Polyuria and polydipsia suggesting central diabetes insipidus
Visual disturbance or ophthalmoplegia from periorbital or orbital infiltration
Rapidly progressive or widespread cutaneous and mucosal disease
Detection of a monoclonal paraprotein on electrophoresis
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous disease is typically persistent and only rarely regresses, following a chronic course; overall prognosis depends on the extent of mucosal, airway and pituitary involvement, and although diabetes insipidus is often transient, airway disease can be life-threatening.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the yellowish papules as eruptive xanthomas and pursuing lipid-lowering treatment despite normal serum lipids.
Failing to enquire about polyuria and polydipsia and thereby missing central diabetes insipidus.
Overlooking upper airway mucosal disease that can progress to obstruction.
Not screening for an associated monoclonal gammopathy.
Expecting spontaneous involution as occurs in juvenile xanthogranuloma, leading to under-monitoring.
references: WHO Classification of Histiocytoses and revised histiocytosis classification (current)
